newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Key facts about the British colony of Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Key facts about the British colony of Hong Kong.

text.p: Hong Kong, Britain's last important colony, reverts to China at midnight on June 30, 1997, when more than 150 years of colonial rule ends.
Here is a profile of the territory followed by a chronology of British colonial rule.
POPULATION - 6.42 million; 98 per cent Chinese.
AREA - 1,074 sq. km (414.6 sq. miles)
CAPITAL - Victoria, name in abeyance, now called Central.

ARMED FORCES: Britain is in the final stages of withdrawing its garrison forces. In mid-1997 all units of the British army, navy and airforce will depart and be replaced by a People's Liberation Army garrison up to 10,000 strong. The HMS Tamar Naval base closed on April 11, and a 40-strong PLA advance guard arrived on April 21. After the handover, internal security will remain the responsibility of the Hong Kong police.

ECONOMY - Hong Kong is rated by the U.S.-based Heritage Foundation as the world's freest economy. It is the world's eighth largest trading entity and the world's busiest container port. Its stock market is the seventh largest worldwide and the second largest in Asia. Its foreign exchange market is the world's fifth largest in terms of daily turnover and its banking system also ranks fifth in external banking transactions.

Following the opening up of China in the 1970s and 1980s, Hong Kong changed from an international manufacturing centre into a service-based economy heavily dependent upon China. Hong Kong's manufacturing centre is now located in southern China, where labour costs are lower.

In 1995, China invested HK$195 billion in Hong Kong and Hong Kong invested HK$624 billion in China. China is also Hong Kong's largest trading partner, accounting for 35 percent of Hong Kong's trade in the first three quarters of 1996.

Under a currency board system the Hong Kong dollar was fixed at 7.80 to one U.S. in 1983. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority was formed in 1994 to manage the Hong Kong dollar. It also controls the Exchange Fund, which held US$71 billion in foreign exchange reserves at the end of January, 1997.
Currency notes are issued by three private commercial banks and an association of banks regulates short-term deposit rates.

In 1996, Hong Kong's economy grew 4.7 percent, the consumer price index rose 6.7 percent, per capita gross domestic product was HK$189,402 (US$24,282) and total exports grew four percent to HK$1,397.9 billion (US$179.22 billion).

In 1997, the government is forecasting economic growth of 5.5 percent and inflation of about seven percent. Total exports are forecast to rise 8.5 percent, with domestic exports static but re-exports rising by 10 percent.

Major industries are ready-to-wear clothes, textiles, basic metals, fabricated metal products and electrical and electronic goods. Major imports are raw materials, semi-manufactures, food and mineral fuels. Tourism was the second largest foreign exchange earner in 1995. Visitor spending totalled HK$72 billion, up 12 percent on 1994, six percent of Hong Kong's GDP.

MODERN HISTORY - Hong Kong means "Fragrant Harbour" in Chinese. It was wrested by Britain from China in three phases starting in the mid-19th century "opium wars". Hong Kong Island went first, under the Treaty of Nanking in 1842. The Kowloon Peninsula was next, by the 1860 Convention of Peking. The rural New Territories, comprising a mainland area adjacent to Kowloon and 235 islands, was added under a 99-year lease in 1898.
Under these treaties, the New Territories, which comprise the bulk of the territory, were to revert to China in 1997.
Sino-British talks on the terms of the handover began in 1982 when China made it known it was intent on resuming sovereignty of the entire territory.

From the 1840s to 1950s, apart from the Japanese military occupation of 1941-45, Hong Kong was mainly a staging post and trans-shipment centre for trade between China and the West. But with the 1950s Korean War and a U.N. embargo on strategic goods to China, most of this trade was cut off and Hong Kong became a manufacturing centre, and later a financing centre.

On December 19, 1984, the Sino-British Joint Declaration, a treaty that agreed that all of Hong Kong would be returned to China at midnight on June 30, 1997, was signed in Beijing. The Basic Law, a mini-constitution for the future Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR), was promulgated by China in 1990.

The Joint Declaration promises Hong Kong will keep its capitalist lifestyle and a high degree of autonomy until 2047. Confidence in that pledge was dented in June 1989 when China's tanks crushed a peaceful democracy movement in Beijing with heavy loss of life. Up to a million Hong Kong people protested, fuelling the growth of Hong Kong's own democracy movement.

After an expansion of democracy by Governor Chris Patten in 1992, the 1995 direct elections gave pro-democracy groups 70 percent of the votes. In December 1996 a 400-member China-picked Selection Committee chose shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa as post-colonial Executive-designate, and created a 60-member provisional legislature to replace the elected Legislative Council, unleashing further quarrels with Britain.
